mstts:express-as.prosody:
Welcome! Have you ever felt your ambition racing ahead of your abilities? If so, you're not alone. In fact, that restless drive to get better—no matter where you start—can turn the simplest talents into something truly extraordinary.
Think about the creative world—or really, any field. Success rarely comes down to pure, natural talent. What really makes a difference? It's the grit to keep improving, the guts to question what's always been done, and the courage to see failure as just another step forward. That's the spirit that Paul Arden, the author whose ideas we'll be exploring together, brings to the table. His perspective nudges us to rethink what greatness really means, showing us that it's our aspirations and our attitude that truly move us ahead.
When we see things this way, the limits we thought we had start to fade. Suddenly, the impossible feels within reach, and every challenge becomes an invitation to try something new. This journey is all about bold choices, creative thinking, and never settling for what everyone else expects.
Imagine shifting your focus away from self-doubt and perfectionism, and channeling it into action and self-belief. That's when the path to real fulfillment—both in your work and your life—becomes so much clearer.
So, as we dive into these ideas inspired by Paul Arden, let's get curious together. What if the desire to improve could outshine the fear of falling short? What if your story was defined not by what is, but by what could be?
I'm excited to explore these possibilities with you. Let's see where this journey takes us.

Chapter 1: Ambition Begins with Wanting More Than What’s Given.
Think back to that moment—maybe early in your own career, or when you first started a creative project—when everything around you felt kind of... set in stone. The rules were clear, expectations were spelled out, and it almost felt like someone else had already mapped your path for you. It’s easy, in those moments, to look at others and think, “Well, they just have it. They’re the naturals.” But, you know, there’s something else bubbling just under the surface—something quieter, but way more powerful. It’s that simple, persistent hunger to reach for more—to do more, to be more—than what you were handed.
Picture this: you’re sitting at your desk, watching as other people get the best assignments, the loudest praise, the biggest chances. You might catch yourself thinking, “Maybe they really are better than me. Maybe I’m missing something.” But here’s the thing—over time, something becomes crystal clear. The folks who move ahead? They aren’t always the most talented in the room. They’re just the ones who want it the most—the ones who actually step up, who aren’t afraid to ask for more, or to risk looking silly if it means growing a little.
Especially in creative fields, this kind of hunger sometimes gets misread. Maybe a junior designer keeps tossing out ideas, even after hearing “not yet” or “that’s not the way we do things.” Colleagues might roll their eyes, but quietly, people notice that persistence. That drive to improve, to contribute, to be part of something bigger—it starts to change the energy of the whole place. It’s not about being the best right from the start. It’s about wanting to get better, and being willing to do what it takes to make that happen.
Real ambition isn’t loud or flashy. It’s that quiet choice to stay late and redo a project. To ask for honest feedback, even when it stings. To volunteer for the tasks nobody else wants. Over time, these small acts—these moments of wanting more—start to add up. The person who keeps reaching, keeps learning, keeps asking? They begin to stand out. Not because they’re born brilliant, but because they’re relentlessly curious and driven.
Most people really underestimate what it means to want something enough to go after it. They wait for a sign, or for someone to tell them they’re ready, or for permission to take the next step. But honestly? Just wanting more—setting your sights higher than what seems possible—creates its own momentum. It opens doors that would’ve stayed shut.
Whether it’s advertising, design, or any creative path you choose, here’s what often separates those who make it from those who don’t: the willingness to want more, to ask for more, and to believe you can always get better. The most successful people aren’t always the most gifted. They’re the ones who refuse to settle for what’s given—and who keep chasing what could be.

Let’s talk about something we all face—mistakes. Chapter Two: Mistakes Are Stepping Stones, Not Roadblocks.
There’s this feeling of dread that creeps in when you mess up, especially if you’re somewhere perfection is expected.
You know that fear—the one that makes you want to just play it safe, stick to what you know, and avoid any risk that could end in failure?
But if you look at the stories of people who really break through, you’ll see something different.
For them, mistakes aren’t the end of the story—they’re actually the start of something new.
Picture this: a team, working into the night on a big campaign. Pressure’s on, the deadline’s close. In the rush, someone makes a call that completely backfires.
The client’s upset, the team’s frustrated, and for a moment, it feels like the whole thing is falling apart.
But then, as the dust settles, something surprising happens.
The team sits down together, picks apart what went wrong, and in doing that, stumbles onto an idea that’s way bolder—and works even better—than their original plan.
That mistake? It wasn’t a disaster. It was actually the spark for a breakthrough.
Most people don’t realize that mistakes are often the only way to figure out what really works.
If you always play it safe, sure, you might avoid feeling embarrassed. But you’ll also shut the door on innovation. The most creative solutions—they don’t come from following the rules perfectly. They come from trial and error, from pushing the boundaries, from having the courage to get it wrong so you can eventually get it right.
Let me share another story. There was this young professional, eager to make a good impression, who took on a project way beyond their experience.
The results? Well, let’s just say it was messy—missed details, awkward presentations, a real sense of being in over their head.
But instead of hiding from those mistakes, they owned up to what went wrong, asked for help, and ended up learning more in those few weeks than they had in years of playing it safe.
Embracing mistakes, seeing them as just part of the journey, became their biggest strength.
In creative industries especially, it’s so easy to let the fear of failure hold you back—to keep you from sharing your ideas, taking risks, or stepping into the unknown.
But if you’re willing to treat every misstep as a lesson, to really see the opportunity in every mistake, you’ll find yourself growing faster, thinking bigger, and reaching higher than those who never take the chance.
It’s easy to forget, but every expert was once a beginner. Every breakthrough started as an experiment. The truth is, the road to success is paved with errors, wrong turns, and rough starts.
What matters isn’t avoiding mistakes—it’s learning from them, and using each one as a stepping stone to something better.

Chapter 3: Thinking Differently Opens Doors Others Don’t See
You know, in a world that really rewards playing it safe, thinking differently can feel like a real gamble. There’s this comfort in sticking with the crowd, doing things the way they’ve always been done. But have you ever noticed something? The most unforgettable work—the stuff that actually changes industries, wins those big awards, or just leaves a mark—almost always comes from people willing to break away from the usual.
Picture this: a creative team’s handed a brief that feels, well... tired. The client says they want something “fresh,” but deep down, they expect the same old approach. Most folks would just deliver what’s asked, stick to the script, and hope not to rock the boat. But then, there’s that one person who speaks up and says, “What if we turned this whole thing upside down?” They start asking questions nobody else even thought about, challenging every assumption, tossing out ideas that seem wild at first. At first, the room’s silent. Maybe even a little skeptical. But then, curiosity takes over. What started as a risky suggestion soon becomes the spark for a campaign that actually stands out.
Here’s something to pay attention to: most of us don’t realize just how fast habits take hold. The longer a team or even just one person keeps doing things the same way, the tougher it becomes to imagine new possibilities. But the folks who really make it in creative fields? They’re the ones who refuse to settle for “that’s just how it’s done.” They hunt for gaps, for contradictions, for that one opportunity to do the unexpected.
There’s a quiet kind of courage in putting a new idea on the table, especially when it goes against the grain. Sure, it might mean facing a bit of criticism—or even falling flat. But over time, being willing to think differently turns into a kind of superpower. It lets you spot solutions others just don’t see, make connections that seem obvious only when you look back.
Think about a designer who’s bored of every project looking the same. Instead of sticking to the usual playbook, they try out a totally new style—even if it doesn’t fit the guidelines. That risk? It pays off. Suddenly, clients who are tired of the ordinary start to notice. The lesson here is pretty clear: innovation hardly ever comes from following the rules. It shows up when you start questioning them, when you’re okay with looking a little foolish, and when you trust that a fresh perspective is worth the leap.
So, in every field, the people who really break through are the ones who see possibilities where everyone else sees limits. They’re not reckless, but they aren’t afraid to challenge the status quo either. By thinking differently, they open doors that would’ve stayed closed—and in the process, they create work that actually matters.

Chapter 4: Confidence, Initiative, and the Power of Asking.
Let’s talk about something that’s easy to overlook, but can make all the difference—getting noticed in a crowded room. You might think it takes being the loudest, or the most talented. But honestly, it’s more about having the confidence to step forward. It’s choosing to take initiative, and then, even if it feels a bit uncomfortable, asking for what you need.
Picture this: someone new joins a team. They’re eager to help, but not quite sure where they fit in. It’s tempting to hang back, just watch and hope that the right chance will show up. But, if you look around, you’ll notice—it’s usually the people who speak up, who put their hands up for the tough assignments, who ask for a chance, that move ahead. It isn’t about arrogance. It’s about believing you can contribute—even if you don’t have every answer yet.
Most folks really underestimate just how powerful it is to ask. A lot of us assume that if something’s meant for us, it’ll just come our way. But here’s the thing: opportunities usually go to the people who make their ambitions known. Think about a manager who’s juggling a million things. Who do you think gets that next big project? The quiet one waiting in the wings, or the person who steps up and says, “Hey, I’d love a shot at that”? The simple act of asking shows you’re ready, willing, and eager to grow.
There’s a story I love about someone in a creative field who felt invisible at work. One day, they decided to go straight to a senior leader with a bold idea. Was the proposal perfect? Not even close. Was the timing ideal? Not really. But the courage to step forward made a lasting impression. The idea wasn’t used, but when a new project came along, guess who that leader remembered? The person who’d had the guts to ask.
Here’s something to keep in mind: confidence doesn’t mean you never doubt yourself. It means you act even when you do. It’s about trusting that your effort and your willingness matter just as much as experience. If you wait for absolute certainty, you’ll probably stay right where you are. But if you move ahead, even when you’re unsure? That’s how you build momentum.
Whether it’s creative work or just everyday life, the willingness to ask—to seek feedback, to request opportunities, to put your ideas out there—can be the difference between standing still and making real progress. It’s not about expecting special favors. It’s about showing that you care about growing, and that you want to be involved.
Over time, making a habit of asking becomes a quiet kind of strength. It helps you build relationships, opens unexpected doors, and gives you a reputation for being someone who takes initiative. Most people never realize just how much can change, just by letting others know what they’re hoping for. The world rarely gives what isn’t asked for. So if you learn to ask, to step forward, to show up, you’ll probably find yourself going further than you ever thought possible.

Let’s dive into Chapter 5: Challenging Limits and Redefining What’s Possible.
You know, every field has its boundaries—those spoken and unspoken rules that tell us what can or can't be done. Most of the time, these limits feel set in stone. But think about it: some of the most remarkable achievements come from people who refuse to accept that something’s impossible. They see limits not as the end, but as the place to start.
Picture a team handed an outrageous brief. The client wants results nobody’s ever pulled off, and the budget? It’s almost a joke. What happens next? Most folks would just lower expectations, talk about what’s realistic, and play it safe.
But every now and then, someone in the room says, “What if we tried anyway?” And that simple question? It changes everything. Suddenly, instead of focusing on what can’t be done, the whole team starts to wonder—what if it actually is possible?
The truth is, most of us don’t even notice how quickly we accept limitations. A project gets labeled “impossible,” and the conversation just... stops there. But the people who really make things happen? They’re the ones who challenge those labels. They ask different questions, look for new resources, and keep going even when things get tough.
There’s this story I love—a designer was told flat out that a certain effect couldn’t be done with the tools they had. Instead of shrugging and moving on, they started experimenting. Sure, they failed a few times. But they kept at it, tried new approaches, and finally cracked the problem. Not only did they solve it, but their workaround actually made the project better. That win wasn’t just about technical skills—it was about refusing to let someone else decide what’s possible.
Especially in creative work, so many of the boundaries we face are self-imposed. We tell ourselves what we can and can’t do, we worry about what’s been done before, or we’re afraid of looking foolish if we try something new. But the people who really break through? They see every “no” as an invitation to give it a shot. And more often than not, they end up achieving way more than they ever expected.
Over time, questioning limits becomes a habit. It leads to breakthroughs, new ways of working, and results that surprise even the most seasoned pros. Most people don’t realize just how much is possible until they actually try. In the end, the difference between ordinary and extraordinary usually comes down to this—are you willing to challenge what everyone else accepts as a given?

Chapter 6: The Value of Sharing Ideas—Generosity Over Guarding
You know, it’s totally natural to want to protect what feels precious. Especially when it comes to creative ideas—sometimes they feel like these fragile little treasures, right? So we hide them away, waiting for the perfect moment to share, or hoping we can polish them until they’re flawless.
But here’s the thing—the world rarely rewards us for keeping our best thoughts locked up. More often, it’s when we actually share those ideas, even if they’re messy or unfinished, that real progress happens. Think about someone you know who’s been quietly working on something, just tweaking and refining in private, always waiting for the ‘right’ time. Days slip into weeks, and that moment of perfection never really arrives. Meanwhile, another person, maybe a bit less worried about everything being just right, throws a rough sketch out to the team. Suddenly, there’s feedback—some of it’s critical, some encouraging, but all of it’s useful. And what happens? The idea starts to grow. It changes, morphs, and before you know it, it’s become something way bigger than it could’ve been alone. Most people don’t realize just how much energy goes into guarding ideas. The fear of being copied, or criticized, or even misunderstood—it can keep us from ever really speaking up. But in reality, it’s the act of sharing that brings ideas to life. Sharing invites collaboration, sparks new connections, and often leads to results no one person could pull off on their own. I once heard about a creative who, after years of holding back, decided to bring a half-formed idea to a team meeting. The response? Well, it was mixed. Some folks saw potential, others just didn’t get it. But then, one person tossed out a suggestion that changed everything. That vague concept suddenly turned into a campaign that ended up winning awards. That story really drives home the point—ideas are meant to be shared, not hidden away. In creative fields, generosity works like a kind of currency. The people who give freely—their thoughts, their time, their encouragement—they always seem to get it back in the most surprising ways. By sharing, you build trust, deepen relationships, and help create a culture where everyone feels comfortable contributing. And over time, making a habit of sharing becomes a real source of strength. It leads to better work, stronger teams, and a genuine sense of belonging that you just can’t find by going it alone. Most people don’t see how much they stand to gain by letting go of the urge to protect, and instead, simply choosing to give.

Chapter 7. Perseverance—Staying the Course When Results Don’t Come Quickly.
There’s this quiet struggle that happens behind every great success story. It’s not flashy, and most people never see it. It’s the long hours, the do-overs, the moments when nothing seems to be working at all.
In a world that’s obsessed with quick wins and overnight breakthroughs, we tend to overlook just how important perseverance really is. But if you talk to anyone who’s achieved something lasting, you’ll hear the same thing: progress almost never follows a straight line.
Think about someone who’s spent months pouring their heart into a project, only to watch it fall flat. It’s tough—not seeing results after all that effort. The easy choice? Give up, move on, chalk it up as wasted time. But the folks who keep showing up, who come back to the work, who don’t let disappointment define them... they’re the ones who eventually break through.
Here’s something to pay attention to: most people have no idea how close they are to a breakthrough when they call it quits. The difference between those who make it and those who don’t? Often, it’s just sticking with it a little bit longer. The process isn’t glamorous. It’s full of setbacks, doubts, and the slow, steady grind of tiny steps forward.
Let me share a story. There was a team that spent years pitching ideas to a potential client. Rejection after rejection. Each time, they’d tweak their approach, take the feedback, and try again. And finally, their persistence paid off. The client not only said yes—they became a long-term partner. Looking back, the team realized the real win wasn’t just landing the deal, but in their willingness to keep showing up, no matter how many times they’d been turned down.
In creative work, perseverance is the real engine that drives growth. It’s what turns raw talent into true skill, and good ideas into something genuinely great. Most people underestimate the power of just not giving up—of being willing to do the work, day in and day out, even when results seem slow or invisible.
Over time, perseverance becomes second nature. It builds resilience, sharpens your expertise, and lays the groundwork for future success. The world’s full of talented people who quit too soon. But the ones who keep going, who trust the process, who believe that effort matters—they end up achieving more than they ever thought possible.

Let’s talk about something that’s often misunderstood— Collaboration: The Magic of Working Together.
You’ve probably heard the old myth about creative genius—the lone visionary, tucked away somewhere, conjuring up brilliance all by themselves. It sounds romantic, right? But, honestly, the best work almost never happens in a vacuum.
Think about it. When different minds get together, when perspectives clash and people actually listen to each other—that’s when something truly original starts to take shape.
Picture a group huddled around a table. Everyone’s got strengths... and blind spots. At first, the conversation might feel a little rough. Ideas bump into each other. Egos get in the way. Things move slowly. But as trust starts to build, something amazing happens. Maybe one person throws out a half-baked idea—and suddenly, it sparks a whole new insight from someone else. Sometimes, a disagreement leads to an unexpected breakthrough. The work gets richer, more layered, more alive than anything one person could’ve pulled off alone.
Most of us don’t even realize just how much we rely on others, even when we think we’re working solo. Every idea takes shape with a little help—from feedback, from context, or even from the invisible influence of people around us. The teams that really shine are the ones who embrace this. They see collaboration not as a compromise, but as a real source of strength.
Here’s a story for you. There was a project that, honestly, looked doomed from the start—too many opinions, too many voices, and not enough direction. But instead of everyone retreating into their own little corners, the team leaned in. They listened, argued, experimented, and eventually found common ground. The end result? It was something none of them could’ve predicted—a campaign that struck a chord way beyond what they’d hoped for.
In creative work, collaboration is the secret ingredient. It takes a good idea and makes it great. It takes a great idea and turns it into something that lasts. Most people don’t realize just how powerful it is to work together—to be open to influence, and to let go of the need to control every single detail.
And here’s the best part: over time, collaboration becomes second nature. It builds trust, deepens relationships, and gives everyone a sense of shared purpose. The world’s full of talented people, but the most remarkable achievements? They almost always come from collective effort.

Let’s dive into Chapter 9—Handling Criticism: Turning Feedback Into Fuel.
You know that sting you feel when someone offers criticism? It’s real, no matter how kindly it’s phrased. Our first instinct is usually to defend ourselves, to explain, or just pull back into what’s comfortable. But here’s the thing—people who really grow? They’re the ones who learn to see feedback not as a threat, but as a genuine gift.
Picture this: you’ve just shared your work with a group, your heart racing, hoping everyone loves it. Instead, you get a mix of reactions—some suggestions, maybe a few doubts, even a pointed question or two. It’s totally normal to feel discouraged in that moment, or to wonder if all the effort was worth it.
But here’s something to pay attention to... Over time, it becomes clear that feedback—even when it’s tough to hear—is exactly what helps us get better.
Most of us don’t even notice how much we resist criticism. Protecting your ego is a strong instinct, especially when the project feels personal. But the people who really succeed? They figure out how to separate themselves from their work. They start to treat feedback as information, not as some kind of verdict on their value.
There’s a story about a designer who got a brutally honest review. For a moment, quitting seemed like the easier option. But instead, they leaned in and asked for details—what worked, what didn’t, and what could be better? Sure, those answers were tough to swallow, but they ended up being the map for real growth. The next project? It was sharper, more focused, and way more effective. The big lesson here is simple: when you embrace criticism, it turns into fuel for progress.
In any creative field, feedback isn’t just likely—it’s guaranteed. The people who really thrive are the ones who seek it out, listen without getting defensive, and use it as a tool to improve. It’s easy to underestimate the power of honest critique, but being open to what’s not working—and then rolling up your sleeves to fix it—that’s where the magic happens.
Over time, making a habit out of welcoming feedback becomes your secret weapon. It leads to faster growth, deeper understanding, and even a reputation for professionalism. The world’s full of folks who avoid criticism. But those who face it head on and use it to get better? They end up going further than they ever imagined.

Chapter 10: The Ongoing Journey—Staying Open, Staying Hungry.
You know, after a few wins, it’s easy to think you’ve made it. Maybe you feel like the hardest part is behind you, and from here on out, the road will be smooth. But the truth? The most rewarding creative lives are built on staying curious, always learning, and always reaching for what’s next.
Imagine someone finally achieving a goal they’ve chased for years. The celebration is amazing, no doubt. But before long, that old itch comes back—the feeling of restlessness. Suddenly, the big question isn’t, “How do I get there?” It becomes, “What else is possible?” Turns out, the journey never really ends. Every milestone just opens up a brand new starting line.
It’s funny—most people don’t even realize how quickly complacency sneaks in. The comfort of routine, the safety of what’s familiar... it can quietly dull your drive. But the folks who keep growing? They’re the ones who stay open. Open to new ideas, new challenges, and even the chance to be a beginner all over again.
There’s this story I love about a creative leader who, after years of success, took on a project in a field they’d never worked in before. The learning curve was steep, the risks were real, and the outcome? Totally uncertain. But that experience lit a new fire—a sense of purpose, excitement, and possibility. The message is crystal clear: what matters just as much as the destination is the journey itself.
In creative work—and honestly, in life—the real magic happens when you keep moving forward. When you stay curious, keep asking questions, and let yourself be open to change, that’s where lasting fulfillment comes from. Most people don’t realize just how powerful it is to stay hungry—to keep reaching for more, no matter how much you’ve grown.
Over time, making learning a habit becomes part of who you are. It brings new opportunities, deeper satisfaction, and a sense of meaning that you just can’t find by playing it safe. The world’s full of people who stop too soon. But those who keep going, who stay open, who stay hungry? They end up living lives richer than they ever imagined.

As we wrap up our time with "It's Not How Good You Are, It's How Good You Want To Be," I just want to say—if you’ve made it to the end, you’re already showing the curiosity and openness that sets you apart.
The lessons we’ve talked about here aren’t just for designers or creatives. They’re for anyone who wants to approach life and work with a little more intention, a little more courage, and a whole lot more possibility.
So, here’s what I hope sticks with you:
Ambition grows when you want more than what the world hands you. Mistakes? They’re not failures—they’re just the raw material for growth and fresh ideas.
Sure, thinking differently comes with risks, but honestly, it’s the only way to stand out.
Asking for what you want? That’s a quiet kind of courage that can really change things.
Most limits are ones we put on ourselves—so challenge them, and you’ll probably surprise yourself.
When you share your ideas freely, you don’t just make your work better—you build deeper connections too.
Perseverance is what separates giving up from breaking through. And when you team up with others, creativity multiplies, and suddenly, what felt impossible starts to seem doable.
If you can welcome criticism, you’ll find it turns into real fuel for getting better.
Staying open and hungry? That’s what keeps your journey meaningful and alive.
The truth is, you don’t have to be the most talented person in the room. You don’t need all the answers, or a spotless track record. What really matters is your willingness to want more, to try, to risk, to learn, and to keep going—especially when things get tough.
The world is shaped by people who show up, who care enough to ask questions, who are brave enough to share, and who never stop reaching for what could be.
So let these ideas guide your next move. Maybe it’s speaking up in a meeting, sharing an idea that’s not quite finished, or simply deciding you’re not going to give up—at least, not today.
Progress is built on small, repeated acts of courage. And you are more capable than you think. The path ahead? It’s wider than it looks.
Keep moving, keep asking, keep growing. The best is always yet to come.
